The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
o:
She needs this seat much

She needs this seat much

more than him because

more than him because

because she is carrying a baby.

because she is carrying a baby.

No Error

No Error
questions.s:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “him” with “he”.

Rule / Concept: Subjective Case in Comparisons -

When we compare two subjects using "than" or "as...as", the pronoun following the comparison should be in the Subjective Case (I, he, she, we, they).

The logic is that the sentence is actually a condensed version of a longer sentence where the verb is "understood." Even if you don't write the verb, the pronoun must remain a subject

In this sentence, we are comparing two people who "need" the seat:

Subject 1: She (needs the seat)

Subject 2: He (needs the seat)

If you complete the sentence mentally, it becomes: "She needs the seat more than he (does)." You would never say "than him does." Therefore, "him" (objective) must be changed to "he" (subjective).

Corrected Sentence - She needs this seat much more than he because she is carrying a baby.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1: My brother is taller than I. (Meaning: than I am).

Example 2: You are as talented as she. (Meaning: as she is).

Example 3: They work harder than we. (Meaning: than we do).

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word segment in the following sentence.
o: they’re coats there
there coats their
their coats their
their coats there
questions.s:
Correct Answer:their coats there

Explanation:

Let’s break down the sentence:
“They are leaving there coats there.”

  • “There” (first use) is wrongly used instead of “their”, which is a possessive pronoun indicating ownership.

  • The second “there” is correct, referring to a place.

Now, let’s evaluate the options:

  • they’re coats there – “they’re” = “they are”; doesn't show possession. ❌

  • there coats their – both uses are incorrect. ❌

  • their coats their – last “their” is incorrect (should be “there”). ❌

  • their coats there – ✅ correct usage: "their" (possessive) + "there" (place).

✅ Final correct sentence:
“They are leaving their coats there.”

questions.q: They enjoyed at the beach, playing volleyball and swimming.
questions.s:
The correct answer is: (a) They enjoyed at

After acquit, avail, reconcile, amuse, resign, avenge, exert, apply, adapt, adjust, pride, absent, and enjoy we use Reflexive Pronouns. In accordance with the rule provided, after the verb "enjoy," we should use the reflexive pronoun "themselves" to indicate that the enjoyment was self-directed.

The corrected sentence is: "They enjoyed themselves at the beach, playing volleyball and swimming."

questions.q:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

The team leader has selected I, you, and him to represent our department in the upcoming competition.
questions.s:
The error is in the order and case of the personal pronouns. Firstly, when listing personal pronouns in a positive context, the polite and standard order is second person (you), third person (him), and then first person (me). Secondly, since the pronouns are the object of the verb 'selected', they must be in the objective case. 'I' is subjective; the objective case is 'me'.

The correct sentence is: The team leader has selected you, him, and me to represent our department in the upcoming competition.

Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

Note:

Personal Pronouns: The pronouns that are used for three persons, namely, the person speaking, the person spoken to, and the person spoken of, are called personal pronouns.

Objective Pronouns: The pronouns me, you, us, him, her, it, and them are called objective pronouns because they act as the objects of verbs and prepositions: Anjali drove us home.
